issues.legal_issue: An admitted signature on a dishonoured cheque gives rise to presumptions of consideration and discharge of a debt or liability, which remain unless the accused raises a probable defence sufficient to rebut them.
material_facts: The accused admitted the signature on the dishonoured cheque and the agreement recording the underlying transaction.
The complainant testified that he had advanced money under an agreement for a proposed sale and that the cheque was issued towards repayment of part of the advance when the sale could not proceed.
The accused did not present rebuttal evidence at trial or raise the later account of coercion in the trial or first appeal; he first raised it during arguments in revision.
The notice demanding payment was received but not answered, and the record did not support the claim that the complainant’s relative had used a position of influence to obtain the signatures.
issues.conclusion: The presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act were not rebutted, so the High Court was wrong to set aside the conviction on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, admission of execution or signature raises rebuttable presumptions that a negotiable instrument was made for consideration and that a cheque was received for discharge of a debt or liability. The accused bears an evidentiary burden to raise a probable defence, assessed on a preponderance of probabilities, and may rely on the complainant’s evidence or other circumstances without testifying. The Court applied K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan, (1999) 7 SCC 510, and the principles summarized in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa, (2019) 5 SCC 418.

rule.if: cheque_dishonour_prosecution and accused_admitted_cheque_signature and complainant_evidence_supported_underlying_transaction and no_probable_rebuttal_defence

predicates.cheque_dishonour_prosecution: The proceeding prosecutes an accused for an offence involving a dishonoured cheque.
predicates.accused_admitted_cheque_signature: The accused admitted signing the cheque on which the prosecution is based.
predicates.complainant_evidence_supported_underlyin: The complainant gave evidence and produced material supporting the transaction said to give rise to the cheque liability.
predicates.no_probable_rebuttal_defence: The accused did not present evidence or circumstances sufficient to make a defence probable.

issues.definition: When a dishonoured-cheque prosecution is supported by an admitted cheque signature and evidence of the underlying transaction, the presumptions remain unrebutted if the accused raises no probable defence.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not set aside concurrent findings in a cheque-dishonour prosecution by accepting a defence first raised in revision and resolving collateral questions about the validity of an agreement that was relied on only to show the underlying transaction.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused and the appellate court upheld the conviction.
The accused first argued in revision that a lawyer’s junior, who was related to the complainant, had used a position of influence to obtain the signatures without payment.
That account had not been raised as a foundation of the defence at trial or in the first appeal, and the record contained no supporting admission or evidence.

The revisional court relied on discrepancies in the agreement’s property details and the complainant’s lack of familiarity with the property, although the agreement had been relied on to show that a transaction occurred, not to determine a claim for specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in accepting the belated account or using collateral defects in the agreement to overturn the concurrent conviction.
issues.legal_principle: The High Court’s revisional jurisdiction is limited and does not justify overturning concurrent findings on a new factual contention lacking a foundation before the trial court. The agreement’s validity as a contract was not the issue in the cheque prosecution; its relevance was limited to showing the transaction underlying the alleged repayment. The Court applied the limited-revisional-power principle discussed in K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1962 SC 1788.

rule.if: cheque_dishonour_prosecution and concurrent_conviction_findings and defense_first_raised_in_revision and revision_court_relied_on_collateral_contract_defects

predicates.cheque_dishonour_prosecution: The proceeding prosecutes an accused for an offence involving a dishonoured cheque.
predicates.concurrent_conviction_findings: The trial court convicted the accused and the first appellate court upheld the conviction.
predicates.defense_first_raised_in_revision: The accused first relied on the relevant factual defence in the revisional proceeding, without having laid its foundation at trial or in the first appeal.
predicates.revision_court_relied_on_collateral_cont: The revisional court relied on defects concerning an agreement that were collateral to whether the cheque liability was established.

issues.definition: In a cheque-dishonour prosecution with concurrent conviction findings, revisional interference is unjustified when it rests on a defence first raised in revision and collateral defects in an agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A custodial sentence for a cheque-dishonour offence may be replaced with a fine where the circumstances make a fine an adequate response, while imprisonment may remain as the consequence of default in payment.
material_facts: The conviction concerned a cheque issued to repay part of an advance in a proposed house sale, rather than an out-and-out commercial transaction.
The complainant’s case was that the accused was in financial distress when the proposed sale was arranged.
A substantial period had passed since the transaction, during which the parties’ social and economic circumstances could have changed.
issues.conclusion: The Court restored the conviction but replaced the immediate term of imprisonment and original fine with an enhanced fine, payable within the specified period, with imprisonment in default; part of the fine was ordered as compensation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the circumstances of the transaction, the passage of time, and the proposition in Kaushalya Devi Massand v. Roopkishore Khore, (2011) 4 SCC 593, that the gravity of a complaint under the Negotiable Instruments Act is not equivalent to that of offences under the Indian Penal Code or other criminal offences. It concluded that an enhanced fine would meet the ends of justice, with imprisonment reserved for default.

rule.if: cheque_dishonour_conviction and transaction_not_commercial and accused_financial_distress and substantial_time_has_passed

predicates.cheque_dishonour_conviction: The accused stands convicted in a prosecution involving a dishonoured cheque.
predicates.transaction_not_commercial: The cheque arose from a transaction that was not an out-and-out commercial transaction.
predicates.accused_financial_distress: The circumstances included the accused being in financial distress in connection with the underlying transaction.
predicates.substantial_time_has_passed: A substantial period passed between the underlying transaction and the sentencing decision.

issues.definition: When a cheque-dishonour conviction arises from a non-commercial transaction involving financial distress and a substantial passage of time, the custodial sentence may be replaced by a fine with imprisonment reserved for default.
